en.title: Europe in the streets: the social contract, migration and the political economy of global unrest
en.deck: A documented reconstruction of Europe's October 2026 protests, the postwar settlement and its crises, housing, wages, public finance, migration, legitimacy, global comparisons and conditional routes for institutional change.
keywords: France Italy Belgium Spain Portugal Albania protests October 2026
European Union migration asylum pact June 2026
European economy inflation housing protests youth
Europe global social unrest political institutions
en.regime: Simultaneous but heterogeneous protests amid housing pressure, public-service discontent and constrained fiscal and political bargaining.
en.key_risk: Confusing distinct grievances and constituencies leads to policies that fail to address housing, public capacity and political responsiveness, while escalation can worsen financing conditions.

contrary_evidence: Spring 2026 Eurobarometer shows majority appreciation of EU membership and 51% trust in the Union; protests are not proof of pan-European rejection.
EU+ asylum applications fell in 2025, contradicting any assertion that rising application counts alone explain current migration politics.
Aggregate EU unemployment remained 6.1% in August 2026; material dissatisfaction cannot be inferred from unemployment alone.
Most 17 October French demonstrations were peaceful; violent episodes cannot be attributed to all protesters.
limitations: News details and participation counts may be revised as investigations and counting progress.
Historical theories are analytic interpretations rather than observational proof of current events.
EU, EU+ and OECD statistics represent different jurisdictions and populations and cannot be combined into one sample.
No controlled identification of a unique protest effect on sovereign yields; global interest-rate and energy shocks are confounders.
No claim that simultaneous worldwide demonstrations are organizationally coordinated, and no electoral-outcome forecasts.
